{{Short description|American physicist (1932–2021)}}
'''Paul Buford Price''' (1932 – 2021<ref name=Death/>), usually known as '''P. Buford Price''', was a [[professor]] in the graduate school at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] and a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].  His work had been wide-ranging over his career, but began with the study of [[physics]] and included [[cosmic rays]], [[astrophysics]], [[nuclear physics]], [[glaciology]], [[climatology]], [[biology]] in extreme environments, and origins of life.  He was born November 8, 1932, in Memphis, TN<ref>{{cite web|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11602031.html|title=Paul Buford Price Biography|publisher=American Institute of Physics}}</ref> and died December 28, 2021.<ref name=Death>{{cite web|url=https://icecube.wisc.edu/news/collaboration/2022/01/p-buford-price-a-pioneer-of-neutrino-astronomy-died-on-december-28-2021/|title=P. Buford Price, a pioneer of neutrino astronomy, died on December 28, 2021|publisher=Ice Cube Collaboration|date=January 4, 2022|author=Silvia Bravo}}</ref>

== Biography ==

In the early part of his career, he codeveloped techniques to record the motions of energetic charged particles in solids, in particular plastics.<ref>{{cite book|author=R.L. Fleischer|author2=P. B. Price|author3=R. M. Walker|title=Nuclear Tracks in Solids|publisher=University of California Press, Berkeley|url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_yfTBvben3GoC|year=1975|isbn=0-520-02665-9|url-access=registration}}</ref>

The technique involves the fact that ionizing particles that traverse materials such as [[Lexan]] plastic break chemical bonds, weakening the material along the path of the particle.  By placing the material in a dissolving solution such as caustic [[sodium hydroxide]], the damage can be dissolved away ["etched"], revealing the ionization damage.  The greater the damage, the faster is the etching. The technique has been used in a number of applications. On the one hand, inspection of the tracks is a valuable tool in determining properties of charged particles as e.g. cosmic rays. On the other hand, the number of such tracks in natural glasses and minerals can be used for [[fission track dating]] of the substance.

A more practical application is the creation of [[nucleopore filter]]s, widely used in microbiology.  To create nucleopore filters, the technique is applied to a polycarbonate film and the etching is allowed to continue from both sides of a sheet of plastic until the two holes are connected, resulting in a tiny hole in the sheet.  Continuous dissolving thereafter slowly and predictably widens the hole diameter until the desired diameter is obtained.

Use of the technique in an  experiment carried by a high-altitude balloon in 1975 resulted in the detection of one highly anomalous cosmic ray particle that traversed a stack of 32 sheets of Lexan plastic. The particle was tentatively identified as a [[magnetic monopole]] in 1975 by Price and some colleagues.<ref>Time magazine, August 25, 1975, "Bring it Back Alive"</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Price|first=P. Buford |author2=E.K. Shirk |author3=W.Z. Osborne |author4=L.S. Pinsky|year=1975|title=Evidence for the Detection of a Moving Magnetic Monopole|journal=[[Physical Review Letters]]|volume=35|issue=8|pages=487–489|doi= 10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.487|bibcode = 1975PhRvL..35..487P }}</ref>  That conclusion was withdrawn in 1978 after further analysis led the Price group to conclude that the particle did not have the appropriate charge to be a monopole,<ref>{{cite journal| author=Price, Shirk, Osborne, Pinsky|journal=[[Physical Review D]]|volume=18|title=Further Measurements and Reassessment of the Magnetic Monopole Candidate|pages=1382–1421|year =1987|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.18.1382|bibcode = 1978PhRvD..18.1382P| issue=5 |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0bt7k5vb}}</ref> though leaving open the possibility that a supermassive magnetic monopole might have caused the track.  However, Luis W. Alvarez proposed that this track can be explained with a platinum atom decaying into osmium and later into tantalum.

Price was a founding member of the team that constructed the [[Antarctic Muon And Neutrino Detector Array]] (AMANDA) and was associated with the [[IceCube Neutrino Detector]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.physics.berkeley.edu/research/faculty/price.html|title=Research Interests|last=Price|first=P. Bufford|publisher=Berkeley University Physics Department|accessdate=2008-11-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070819210123/http://physics.berkeley.edu/research/faculty/Price.html|archive-date=2007-08-19|url-status=dead}}</ref> During his work with AMANDA, he showed that micrometre-size bacteria and archaea can live in liquid veins throughout depths of several kilometers in glacial ice.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Price|first=P. Buford|date=February 1, 2000|title=A habitat for psychrophiles in deep Antarctic ice|journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]|volume=97|issue=3|pages=1247–1251|doi=10.1073/pnas.97.3.1247|bibcode = 2000PNAS...97.1247P|pmid=10655516|pmc=15584|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 1971, he received the [[Ernest O. Lawrence Medal]] with [[Robert M. Walker (physicist)|Robert Walker]] and Robert Fleischer for work on understanding how to capture charged particle tracts in solids.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sc.doe.gov/lawrence/html/Laureates/1970s/robertl.htm|title=The Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award - Robert L. Fleischer, P. Buford Price, Robert M. Walker, 1971|publisher=US Department of Energy Office of Science|accessdate=2008-11-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080921201821/http://www.sc.doe.gov/lawrence/html/Laureates/1970s/robertl.htm|archive-date=2008-09-21|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1975.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://physics.berkeley.edu/index.php?option=com_dept_management&act=people&Itemid=299&limit=50&limitstart=0&task=view&id=12|title=physics@berkeley: P. Buford Price|publisher=Berkeley University Physics Department|accessdate=2008-11-16}}</ref>
